rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remaining Christians follow Paul and divided into sects, with Catholics and Protestants the leading denominations.
rows.anchor: The rest were the followers of Paul and continued to divide into various sects. The most prominent among them are the Catholics and the Protestants.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assembly of the terrible day is the prophets' testimony before God about their peoples, illustrated by Jesus' testimony concerning Christians.
rows.anchor: refer to that great testimony of the prophets which they will bear on the Day of Judgement before God regarding their people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Jesus bears this testimony, Christians will be ashamed before him and God and face devastation and mourning.
rows.anchor: the Christians will feel ashamed to face both him and God. Nothing will then remain for them except devastation and mourning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic expressions convey wonder: although the reality is made palpable today, people neither listen nor hear; their full perception on Judgment Day comes too late.
rows.anchor: are meant to express wonder in Arabic. The implication is that today when the reality is sounded and made palpable to them, they neither listen nor hear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When people come before God, they will see and hear fully, but it will be too late; the wrongdoers are those who wrong themselves and remain spiritually blind and deaf.
rows.anchor: No one would be more aware of them at that time. However, it would be too late to listen and to see: they would be doomed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day of Longing is the great assembly, when perception opens but repentance, reform, and repair are closed; heedless unbelievers will wish to return to do good, without success, and face their deeds' consequences.
rows.anchor: everyone’s eyes will be opened but the doors to repentance, reformation and making up will be closed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone will rule that day; all return to Him, no one can help another, and intercession occurs only with His permission.
rows.anchor: None will be in a position to help anyone and without God’s permission no intercession will take place.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophets' accounts show Christians that earlier prophets taught Muhammad's message, while warning Quraysh that Abraham's and Ishmael's religion differs from what they now follow; the Qur'an presents Abraham's true religion.
rows.anchor: The real religion of Abraham (sws) is the one which the Qur’ān is presenting before them.

none: Translation and verse text only; no distinct commentary point.
Translation and verse text only; no distinct commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who wish to inherit Abraham's standing must sincerely fulfill the covenant made with God through him; lineage alone does not make them worthy successors.
rows.anchor: this is only possible if with full sincerity they fulfil what they promised God through Abraham (sws).

rows.speaker: Most exegetes
rows.claim: Most exegetes understand the Book here as the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: Most exegetes interpret the book to be the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi prefers the previous scriptures, specifically the Torah and Gospel, as the Book; the shared prophetic teaching shows Qur'an-deniers also deny their own prophets and scriptures.
rows.anchor: in my opinion, it refers to previous scriptures. Here and in later verses too where the accounts of the prophets are mentioned, it refers to the Torah and the Gospel.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Book means Qur'an, the accounts instruct the prophets' followers; benefiting from them is a blessing, while failure to benefit deprives them of God's favor without harming anyone else.
rows.anchor: the accounts of these prophets should be narrated to those who are their followers so that they learn a lesson.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Either interpretation leaves the verse's overall implication largely unchanged.
rows.anchor: In either of the two interpretations, the overall implication of the verse will not change much.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's uprightness rebukes the People of the Book and Arabian idolaters for inventing a religion while claiming his lineage and legacy; he was sincere and passed God's tests.
rows.anchor: the People of the Book and the Idolaters of Arabia are being rebuked on inventing a whole new religion in spite of claiming to be Abraham’s progeny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's tested character, rather than descent, grounds leadership: his covenant excludes the unjust, so only descendants who uphold his character can inherit his standing.
rows.anchor: In recognition of his success in these tests, he was given the title of ṣiddīq (upright) by God and was bestowed the leadership of nations by Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's descendants who embrace injustice, polytheism, or disbelief have no share in his status, whether descended through Isaac or Ishmael; ṣiddīq's implications are essential to the verse's meaning.
rows.anchor: Those who are unjust to their souls and become proponents of polytheism and disbelief will have no share in it, whether they are from the progeny of Isaac (sws) or Ishmael (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated address Father shows Abraham's compassionate, affectionate concern for his misguided father throughout the argument.
rows.anchor: shows how compassionately and affectionately he spoke to him.

rows.speaker: Jews
rows.claim: The Jews claim that Āzar was Abraham's paternal uncle rather than his father.
rows.anchor: not his paternal uncle, as claimed by the Jews.

rows.speaker: our exegetes
rows.claim: The source says exegetes accepted the claim that Āzar was Abraham's uncle without much deliberation.
rows.anchor: This opinion has been accepted without much deliberation by our exegetes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects the uncle identification and holds Āzar was Abraham's father; he says later Sabā’ī writers turned the claim into propaganda.
rows.anchor: Āzar is the name of Abraham’s (sws) father and not his paternal uncle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says later Sabā’ī writers made propaganda from the uncle claim and notes that he had refuted the Torah's account earlier.
rows.anchor: Later the Sab ā’ī’s have created a propaganda from it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham first argues that handmade idols cannot hear, see, or help, making idolatry foolish and contrary to intellect and human nature.
rows.anchor: clearly shows that it is blatant foolishness and has no relation to intellect and human nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham next argues that assigning partners to God cannot rest on conjecture; he offers revealed knowledge in place of unsupported belief.
rows.anchor: The second thing he has said is that determining God’s partners is not a matter of conjecture.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nature, intellect, and the world testify to one God, while partners lack evidence; only revelation supplies true knowledge, and Abraham's straight path means monotheism leading directly to God.
rows.anchor: Every person who is upright is compelled to believe in Him but what is the compulsion in believing in His partners without any reason?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's deepest enmity is toward monotheism; obeying God's rebel is equivalent to worshipping him, so following Satan abandons God.
rows.anchor: the greatest malice and enmity the latter has is for the straight path of monotheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham says his father could have pleaded ignorance before guidance arrived, but revelation removes that excuse; he fears punishment and the fate of Satan's allies.
rows.anchor: until then they had an excuse that God’s guidance had not reached them but now that it has reached them, they do not have any excuse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's promise to seek forgiveness despite his father's callousness exemplifies his softness, sympathy, and love.
rows.anchor: the promise by Abraham (sws) to pray for his forgiveness shows how soft, sympathetic and loving he was.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's declaration of disavowal shows his lack of concern for public opinion and his trust in God.
rows.anchor: lack of concern at what people would say and trust in God is evident from every word of this declaration

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Salām is an affectionate farewell formula as well as a blessed greeting when people meet.
rows.anchor: greet people when meeting them, at the time of departing too it is a very affectionate way of expressing farewell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of God as ḥafī means affectionate, caring, and kind; Abraham's offer to pray for his hostile father shows his tenderness, and he continued until God stopped him.
rows.anchor: The word ﺣَrefers to someone who is very affectionate, caring and kind.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's promise to seek forgiveness demonstrates his love despite his father's callousness; Qur'anic instances show he kept praying until God stopped him.
rows.anchor: he kept making this prayer until the Almighty stopped him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite his kindness, Abraham would not compromise through fear or courtesy: he formally disavowed his family and their deities.
rows.anchor: He did not offer any compromise because of his gracious behaviour or because of any fear and expressly declared his acquittal from them and from their deities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural form extends Abraham's disavowal beyond his father to his companions, associates, family, and the deities they invoke; he then affirms worship of God alone.
rows.anchor: not only proclaimed acquittal from his father but also from all his companions, associates and members of the family.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's closing confidence expresses trust that God will guide and support him; the preacher of truth must combine softness with firmness.
rows.anchor: It is in fact this amalgam of soft and stern attitude which distinguishes a preacher of truth from others.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's declaration amounted to migration, and he left his people after proclaiming his disavowal.
rows.anchor: tantamount to migration. Thus after this proclamation he migrated from them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omission of Ishmael seems striking because he fathered the Ishmaelites, including Muhammad as God's final prophet.
rows.anchor: to them belonged Muḥammad, the last and final prophet of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naming Jacob with Isaac highlights three successive prophets—Abraham, his son, and grandson; adding Joseph shows a prophetic family unmatched in human history.
rows.anchor: the father, the son and the grandson were all prophets.

rows.speaker: Imām Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī argued that Ishmael was the greatest blessing granted through Abraham's migration.
rows.anchor: the greatest blessing of migration – as proven by my mentor Imām Farāhī in his book Fī man huwa al-dhabīḥ – was Ishmael (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi explains Ishmael's omission from this list by noting that he was already mentioned independently so the primarily addressed Arabian idolaters would focus on their ancestor.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, the reason for this lack of mention is that he is mentioned ahead independently.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zacharias' story prepares for Jesus, and Abraham's old-age childbearing provides another miraculous-birth example; therefore miraculous birth does not justify divinity.
rows.anchor: examples of miraculous birth are exist before the times of Jesus (sws) too. Ascribing divinity to someone just because of this reason is mere foolishness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's mercy here includes all blessings granted to Abraham and his descendants, including prophethood and messengerhood.
rows.anchor: all the blessings and favours received by Abraham (sws) and his progeny including prophethood and messengerhood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lisān ṣidq means enduring fame and reputation; God amplified Abraham's preaching so his honor persisted for millennia, culminating in Muhammad's revival of Abraham's mission.
rows.anchor: As a result, that fame and loftiness has become eternal.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham prayed for later generations to remember him fondly; Islahi connects this supplication to the lasting fame described in the preceding verse.
rows.anchor: And let those who come later continue to fondly remember me.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses follows Abraham as a celebrated prophet among Isaac's descendants and served as messenger and prophet to Pharaoh, his nation, and the Israelites.
rows.anchor: he was sent in this capacity both to the Pharaoh (sws) and his nation and to the Israelites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mukhlasan denotes a person chosen for a special task; while every prophet is chosen, Moses alone receives this Qur'anic title because of his unique conversation with God.
rows.anchor: the answer to this question is that this distinction relates to his singular status in conversing with God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ayman can mean the right side or the sacred and blessed side; Islahi prefers sacred and blessed, following the parallel account of the sacred valley of Tuwā.
rows.anchor: In my opinion here it refers to the latter meaning. This is evident from parallel verses of the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Najiy describes secret whispering or a trusted confidant; Moses' direct conversation with God, ordinarily mediated through Gabriel for prophets, was his unique distinction.
rows.anchor: whenever God has spoken to his prophets, it is through His trusted angel Gabriel; never directly.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even in this encounter Moses could not see God, since humans, jinn, and even mountains cannot endure God's manifested splendor; Sūrah Ṭāhā gives the conversation's details.
rows.anchor: no human being or jinn or even inanimate objects like mountains have the capacity to tolerate the splendour of God manifesting before them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron's prophetic assistance was a divine favor, uniquely granted to Moses at his request because of the burden of confronting Pharaoh and organizing the Israelites.
rows.anchor: This help was not something voluntary on the part of Aaron (sws). He was deputed by a God as His prophet.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God accepted Moses' prayer for Aaron to share his mission; the Qur'an presents Moses as free of the grave sins Jews attributed to him.
rows.anchor: God accepted this prayer of Moses and this has been mentioned in S ūrah Ṭāhā as a great favour.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmael heads Abraham's other prophetic branch, from whom Muhammad is the final prophet; the account challenges Quraysh's claim to his legacy while they oppose the Qur'an's Abrahamic message.
rows.anchor: The first prophet in this branch was Ishmael (sws) and the last was Mu ḥammad (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣādiq al-waʿd refers especially to Ishmael's consent to Abraham's sacrifice dream and his steadfast submission until God stopped the test; both were judged upright and sincere.
rows.anchor: When the time of fulfulling this promise arrived, without any reluctance, he placed his neck below the knife of his father.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The compact phrase portrays faith's peak: a servant keeps his promise to God and is ready to sacrifice his life, exposing the hollow boasting of descendants seeking worldly advantage.
rows.anchor: A servant of God who is true to what he has promised to Him and is prepared to sacrifice his life for it has truly attained the pinnacle of faith and submission to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmael's command to pray and give zakāh sums up duties to God and people; all religious law rests on these practices, and neglecting them means neglecting religion.
rows.anchor: these two worship rituals comprehensively signify the all the rights of God as well as those of human beings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being pleasing to God comprehensively praises Ishmael as exactly the servant God wants; the source adds that Jewish hostility distorted Abraham's and Ishmael's history and concealed Ishmael's story.
rows.anchor: the Almighty himself bears witness that he conforms to His liking.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says Jewish hostility led them to distort Abraham's and Ishmael's history and especially to hide Ishmael's history.
rows.anchor: they had hidden the history of the latter in such a way so that no one is able to get wind of it.
